855.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
855.hook: a man hangs upside down in a well, a serpent below, an elephant above, and he reaches for a drop of honey
855.howItsDone: Vidura's parable of the man in the well is retold in Hindu teaching and storytelling as a picture of life held between time and desire.

segments.voice: Yesterday the night book, Sauptika, ended by the Ganga, with two sages between the weapons and a jewel carried home to Draupadi. Did you get to say a calm word? Today, the book of the women. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

A traveler is lost in a thick forest full of wild animals. Running from them, he falls into a well, but he doesn't hit the bottom. He's caught by creepers and hangs there, upside down. Below him, at the bottom of the well, waits a great serpent. Above him, at the well's mouth, stands a dark elephant. Rats are gnawing at the roots of the tree that holds the creepers. And from a honeycomb in the branches, a drop of honey falls toward his mouth. Today, the start of Stri, the book of the women, where Vidura tells this story to a grieving king.
screen: `A MAN HANGS IN A WELL.` → `A SERPENT BELOW.` → `A DROP OF HONEY.`

segments.voice: The war is over. In Hastinapura, the old blind king Dhritarashtra has heard that Duryodhana and his brothers are dead, and he falls to the ground in grief. His half-brother Vidura, the wise one who warned him again and again, sits with him. And instead of an argument, Vidura tells a story: the man in the well. In Ganguli's telling, what does the man do, hanging there between the serpent and the elephant, with the rats chewing the roots? He drinks the honey. And he wants more. He still wishes to live, and he still wants the sweetness. Then Vidura explains. The forest is the world we wander in. The wild animals are illnesses. The well is the body. The serpent at the bottom is Time, which takes everything. The elephant is the year, the rats are the days and the nights eating away at our time, and the creepers are the hope of life that holds us. The honey is the pleasures we keep reaching for, even here. Vidura isn't mocking the man. He's describing everyone, the king included. And his counsel to Dhritarashtra is gentle and hard at once: every living being comes to this; grief cannot bring your sons back; let the wise not be swept away by it. It's a strange way to open a book of mourning. Before the women walk out onto the field to find their dead, the story pauses on a man in a well, still tasting the honey.
screen: `THE KING HEARS THE NEWS` · `VIDURA TELLS A STORY` · `HE STILL WANTS THE HONEY` · then, large: `THE WELL IS THE WORLD`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and notice the breath going in and out by itself. The story counts time in days and nights. This breath is part of today, and it's here now. Breathe in, and notice one sweet thing in this moment: warmth, light, a sound, the chair holding you. Breathe out, and let it be enough. Then let the next breath come, and notice another. If you pray, you can give thanks in your prayer for this one breath. The bell holds the time.
Stri. The book of the women begins with a grieving king and Vidura's story of a man in a well, still reaching for the honey.
Your line: Stri: Gandhari's curse. Today, when you notice yourself reaching for the next sweet thing, pause and taste the one you have. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

856.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
856.hook: a blind king asks to embrace the man who killed his sons, and Krishna slides an iron statue into his arms
856.howItsDone: The iron Bhima appears in retellings of the Stri Parva as a picture of a father's grief and of Krishna's foresight.

segments.voice: Your line: Stri: Gandhari's curse. Yesterday Vidura told the grieving king about a man in a well, still reaching for the honey. Did you taste the sweet thing you already had? Day eight hundred fifty-six.

A line of chariots and carts leaves Hastinapura, and behind it walk the women of the royal house, weeping, their hair unbound. They're going out to the battlefield to find their dead. At the front is Dhritarashtra, the blind old king, with Gandhari beside him. On the road, the Pandavas come to meet him: the five brothers who won, with Krishna. They bow. The king has to greet them. And he asks for one of them in particular. Today, an embrace that isn't what it seems.
screen: `THE WOMEN WALK OUT.` → `THE PANDAVAS COME TO MEET HIM.` → `HE ASKS FOR ONE.`

segments.voice: Dhritarashtra embraces Yudhishthira first, the text says, without joy. Then he asks for Bhima. Bhima is the one who killed Duryodhana and Duhshasana, the one who made the vows and kept them. Krishna understands what's in the old man's heart. So he quietly pushes Bhima aside and moves forward an iron statue of Bhima. Duryodhana had it made, in Ganguli's telling, to practice against with his mace. The blind king takes the iron figure in his arms, and he crushes it. He's so strong, and so full of grief and rage, that the statue breaks apart, and he hurts himself doing it. He falls to the ground, and Sanjaya lifts him up. And then Dhritarashtra weeps, crying out for Bhima, sure he has just killed him. Krishna speaks. It was not Bhima, he says, in effect. It was an image of iron. I knew what you meant to do. Your sons died because of their own deeds and because you didn't stop them. The king is ashamed, and maybe relieved. He washes, and then he embraces the brothers, Bhima too, with blessings this time. Look at the order of things here. A father's grief is so strong it could kill. Krishna doesn't shame him in front of everyone or refuse the embrace. He gives the grief something to break that isn't a person. And only after it breaks can the real embrace happen.

857.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
857.hook: the Pandavas walk toward the mother whose sons they killed, and she has the power to burn them
857.howItsDone: Storytellers, dance-dramas and modern retellings often return to Gandhari's meeting with the Pandavas, and some readers single out her answer to Duryodhana, where dharma is, there is victory, as the heart of her character.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, the blind king crushed an iron Bhima, and only then embraced the living one. Did your anger find somewhere to go first? Today, the victors have to face a mother. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

The winners of the war have a visit to make, and nobody wants to make it. The five Pandava brothers, with Krishna beside them, have to go and stand in front of Gandhari. She is the queen whose sons fell to them on that field. She has kept her eyes bound with a cloth for her whole married life, the story says, and her years of discipline have given her a power the brothers fear. Her anger could burn. Before they arrive, the sage Vyasa comes to her first. Today, what a grieving mother says to the men who won, and what one glance does.
screen: `THE WINNERS MUST VISIT.` → `A MOTHER WITH BOUND EYES.` → `VYASA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Vyasa reminds Gandhari of something she said herself. All through the war, when Duryodhana came to ask for her blessing, she gave him the same answer: where dharma is, there victory is. She didn't bless him with victory. Now, Vyasa says, the words came true. Don't let anger undo them. So she holds the curse back, but she still has a question, and she puts it to Bhima. Why did you strike my son below the navel, against the rules of the mace fight? Bhima doesn't pretend. He says, in Ganguli's telling, that he was afraid, that Duryodhana could not be beaten fairly, and he reminds her what her son did to Draupadi in the hall. Then she asks the harder thing: did you really drink Duhshasana's blood? Bhima answers that it never passed his lips. Then Gandhari asks for the king. Yudhishthira comes forward, trembling, hands joined, and says it plainly: I killed your sons. Curse me. Gandhari says nothing. But through a small gap in the cloth over her eyes, her gaze falls on the tips of his toes, and his nails, which were fine before, turn dark and damaged. Arjuna, watching, steps behind Krishna. And then her anger passes. She comforts them the way a mother would and sends them to their own mother, Kunti. One look through a sliver of cloth, and that's all the burning there is. The book is named for women, and here a woman holds the power to burn the winners, and mostly chooses not to use it.
screen: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY` · `BHIMA ANSWERS HONESTLY` · `"CURSE ME"` · then, large: `ONE GLANCE AT HIS TOES`

858.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
858.hook: the queen who chose not to see is given sight, and the first thing she sees is the battlefield
858.howItsDone: Gandhari's lament on the battlefield, spoken to Krishna, is read and retold as a passage of mourning, and some modern plays and poems take it up.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari held back her curse, and only one glance through her blindfold escaped. Did you let a breath go by before something sharp? Today, she sees. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

For years Gandhari has lived behind a cloth she tied on herself. Now the sage Vyasa gives her what the text calls a celestial sight, a way to see far beyond where she stands. She doesn't use it to look at the sky, or at the palace, or at the faces of the Pandavas. She turns it on the field of Kurukshetra, where the war just ended. And standing beside her is Krishna, the one person she will speak to about all of it. Today, what Gandhari sees, and the women she sees there.
screen: `A CLOTH SHE TIED HERSELF.` → `VYASA GIVES HER SIGHT.` → `SHE LOOKS AT THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: What she sees first isn't warriors. It's women. Wives, mothers and daughters of both armies, moving across the field, searching. Some have never walked outside the women's quarters before, and now they're out among the dead, hair loose, calling names. Gandhari describes it all to Krishna, one scene after another. Stri means woman, and here the epic hands the women the story. She sees Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, bending over him and talking to him as if he could still hear. She sees her own daughter, Duhshala, running here and there, looking for her husband Jayadratha and unable to find his head. She sees her son Duryodhana lying on the ground, and his wife beside him. She sees Karna, and the women grieving him too. And she keeps turning to Krishna. Look at this, she says. Look at her. Notice what she's doing. Through all of it, she isn't counting victories or losses for one side. The women she describes come from both camps, and their grief sounds the same. A Pandava widow and a Kaurava widow, in this book, are doing exactly the same thing in the dust. The war books spent chapter after chapter on who killed whom. Stri spends its time on who's left to bury them. Grief has been building in Gandhari all this time, and it will break by the end of her speech. But that's tomorrow. Today she simply looks, and makes Krishna look with her.
screen: `SHE SEES THE WOMEN FIRST` · `UTTARA, DUHSHALA, DURYODHANA'S WIFE` · `GRIEF FROM BOTH CAMPS` · then, large: `"LOOK, KRISHNA"`

859.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
859.hook: a grieving mother turns to Krishna and curses him, and he answers with something close to a smile
859.howItsDone: Gandhari's curse on Krishna is told in temple discourses, plays and retellings of the epic, and storytellers link it to the later end of Krishna's own clan.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari was given sight and turned it on the women searching the field. Did you notice who was left cleaning up after a fight? Today, the curse. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

She has been talking to Krishna the whole time. Look at this widow, look at that mother, look at my son. And somewhere in that long walk across the field, the grief turns. Gandhari stops describing and starts accusing. You could have stopped this, she says to him. You had the power. You had the words. Both sides listened to you, and you let it happen. This is the curse in our title, and it isn't aimed at the Pandavas. It's aimed at Krishna himself, standing right next to her. Today, what Gandhari says, and how Krishna takes it.
screen: `THE GRIEF TURNS.` → `"YOU COULD HAVE STOPPED THIS."` → `THE CURSE IS FOR KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Gandhari reaches for the power her discipline has given her, the power she held back with Yudhishthira. Because you stood by while the Kurus and the Pandavas destroyed each other, she says, your own people will destroy each other. Your kinsmen, the Vrishnis, will kill one another. You yourself will die alone, in a wild place, by an inglorious means. And the women of your house will weep over their dead, the way the women of my house are weeping now. She has just spent this book looking at grieving women. Now she wishes that same scene on Krishna's family. Then the surprise. Krishna doesn't argue. He doesn't defend himself or explain the war. In Ganguli's telling he answers with a kind of calm, almost a smile. I already knew this, he says, in effect. My people can't be destroyed by anyone else, and they will destroy themselves. You've only spoken what was going to happen. And then he turns her own grief back to her, gently. The war came, he says, from your son's choices, and from your own failure to restrain him. Get up. Don't give yourself to sorrow. Gandhari falls silent. So the curse lands, and Krishna accepts it. The book doesn't settle whether she was right to blame him. It lets a mother say something almost unsayable to Krishna, whom the epic honors as God, and lets him take it without striking back. The epic will come back to this curse. For now, it simply hangs in the air over the field.

If you pray, you can bring that question into your prayer just as it is. The bell holds the time.

860.title: Stri: Gandhari's curse
860.hook: at the river, with water in their hands for the dead, Kunti finally tells her sons who Karna was
860.tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
860.howItsDone: Hindu rites after a death can include offering water for the dead, often at a river, and retellings of the Mahabharata return to the moment at the Ganga when Kunti names Karna as her son.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari cursed Krishna, and he took the curse without striking back. Did someone's grief come out as blame near you? Today, the last scene of the book of the women. Day eight hundred sixty.

Water is the last thing the living can give the dead. After the fires on the field are lit, the whole household walks down to the Ganga: the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, the widows of both sides. They step into the river, and one by one they offer water for each person they lost, a father, a brother, a son, a teacher. It's a quiet, orderly rite after so much noise. And in the middle of it, Kunti speaks up and tells her sons something she has carried for their whole lives. Today, the water, and Kunti's secret.
screen: `THE FIRES ARE LIT.` → `EVERYONE GOES TO THE GANGA.` → `KUNTI SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Kunti asks her sons to offer water for one more warrior: Karna. The brothers are puzzled. Karna was the enemy, the charioteer's son, the man Arjuna killed. Why him? And Kunti tells them. He was your eldest brother. He was my son, born to me from the sun god before I married your father. I set him adrift as a baby, and I never told you. The Pandavas are stunned. Yudhishthira is crushed. Soon after, as the next book opens, he remembers how Karna's feet resembled Kunti's, the text says, and how his anger used to drain away when he looked at them. Now he understands why. He grieves for the brother he fought without knowing, and the brother who, he realizes, could have been on his side all along. He offers the water for Karna himself, and brings Karna's family into the rites. The book of the women opened with a blind king's grief. It closes with a woman's word changing what the men thought the war was. Gandhari held back a curse, then spoke one. The widows walked the field. And Kunti, at the river, says the thing that turns the victory upside down. The warrior whose fall they had cheered was their own brother. That's Stri: a book where the women speak, and the winners learn what their victory cost.
screen: `"OFFER WATER FOR KARNA"` · `"HE WAS YOUR ELDEST BROTHER"` · `YUDHISHTHIRA REMEMBERS HIS FEET` · then, large: `THE WOMEN SPEAK LAST`

segments.voice: Yesterday Stri ended at the river, where Kunti told her sons that Karna was their brother. Did you say a kind word about someone absent? Today, the end of the week, and a new book. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

Yudhishthira has everything he fought for, and he doesn't want any of it. The kingdom is his. His enemies are gone. And he tells his brothers he's leaving for the forest, to live as a hermit. A kingdom bought with the deaths of teachers, cousins and a brother he never knew is not something he can bear to rule. His brothers argue. Draupadi argues. Sages come and argue, and at last he lets himself be crowned. But the grief and doubt don't leave him. So Krishna does something different. He takes Yudhishthira to the field, to the one teacher still alive there: Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows. Today, how the new book opens.
screen: `HE WON, AND WANTS TO LEAVE.` → `NOBODY CAN MOVE HIM.` → `KRISHNA TAKES HIM TO BHISHMA.`

segments.voice: These next two books, Shanti and Anushasana, are mostly one long conversation. Shanti means peace. Anushasana means instruction. And the peace being sought is Yudhishthira's own, the peace of a man who can't live with what he's won. The surprise is who does the teaching. Krishna is there, and Krishna is God in this story. Yet he steps back. He gives Bhishma relief, so that the pain of the arrows, the weariness and the confusion leave him, and his mind becomes clear, with all he ever learned ready to hand. Bhishma asks, in effect, why me? You could teach him yourself. Krishna's answer, in Ganguli's telling, is that he wants these words to come from Bhishma, so that Bhishma's fame will last as long as the world does. Then there's Yudhishthira himself. He hangs back. He's ashamed. He's the one whose side brought this old man down, and he's afraid to come close. Bhishma has to call him forward and tell him he has nothing to fear. So look at the scene. A dying man on a bed of arrows. A ruler who can't forgive himself, asking the man he wounded how to live. And God standing to one side, letting the human being speak. That's how this whole stretch works. Over the next sessions we'll take a few selections from what Bhishma says: about kings, about hard times, about guests and blame, and about letting go. This week began with Vidura's man in the well, still reaching for the honey. It ends with a grieving king at the bedside of a teacher.
screen: `SHANTI: PEACE. ANUSHASANA: INSTRUCTION.` · `KRISHNA GIVES BHISHMA CLARITY` · `YUDHISHTHIRA HANGS BACK` · then, large: `GOD LETS BHISHMA TEACH`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one person who taught you something real, a parent, a teacher, a friend, an elder. Breathe in, and picture yourself sitting at their side. Breathe out, and let one question you'd ask them now come up. You don't need the answer. If there's shame or distance between you, let that sit here too. If you pray, you can hold that person and your question in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shanti and Anushasana. Peace, and instruction: the two books where Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira from the bed of arrows.
